Welcome to Part 2. In Part 1 we covered the architecture and licensing. Here’s the operational truth that follows: MDVM only protects what it can see. Discovery and inventory aren’t glamorous, but they’re the foundation everything else stands on. A flawless prioritization engine running over a 60%-complete inventory will give you a 60%-complete answer. Worse, it will give it to you with full confidence, which is the dangerous kind of wrong.
So let’s get specific about Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management device discovery: what MDVM can see, what it can’t, and how to extend its reach.
The Three Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Device States When you open the Defender XDR portal and go to Assets → Devices, every device you see is in one of three states:
Managed. Onboarded to Defender for Endpoint. The MDE sensor is running, telemetry is streaming, and you’re getting full vulnerability and configuration assessment. This is the gold-standard state and where MDVM earns its money.
Discovered (unmanaged). MDVM noticed it on the network, but it’s not onboarded. You’ll get IP, MAC, OS guess, and sometimes open-port information from passive discovery. You won’t get vulnerability assessment unless you do something about it (we’ll get there).
Excluded. You explicitly told MDVM to ignore the device. Useful for honeypots, certain test systems, and devices outside your scope.
The work in Part 2 is mostly about moving devices from the “discovered” column to the “managed” column, or (when that’s not possible), running authenticated scans against them to get vulnerability data without an agent.
Passive Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Device Discovery This is on by default and you almost never want to turn it off. The MDE sensor on managed devices passively listens for network signals like ARP, DHCP, mDNS, network connection metadata, and reports unknown hosts back to the cloud. Defender XDR aggregates these reports across all your sensors and gives you a list of unmanaged devices with a confidence score on what they probably are.
Two things to know.
It’s passive only. The sensor isn’t sending probes; it’s just listening to traffic that already crosses its NIC. This means it’s safe in OT environments, there’s no scan stimulus that could upset a fragile PLC. (For the OT readers: yes, this is the part you want. We’ll come back to OT considerations in Part 4.)
It only sees what your sensors can see. If you have one MDE-onboarded laptop on the corporate VLAN and a hundred IoT devices on a separate isolated VLAN with no managed endpoint on it, MDVM will see one device. Your VLAN structure determines your discovery surface.
There’s also a standard discovery mode, which is more active, the sensor occasionally probes unknown devices to fingerprint them more accurately. It’s safer than it sounds (Microsoft tuned it heavily), but in OT and ICS environments I default to passive only and document the decision — a position consistent with NIST SP 800-82 Rev 3 guidance on minimizing scan stimulus in operational technology networks.
Software inventory For every managed device, MDVM enumerates installed software and versions. The Defender XDR portal exposes this as Software inventory, a tenant-wide, deduplicated list of every product/version combination across your fleet, with weakness and CVE counts attached.
This is more useful than people realize. A few real-world queries it answers in seconds:
“How many machines are running Java 8u202?” (Spoiler: more than you want.) “Which software vendors am I most exposed through?” “Where is product X deployed?”, for incident response when a CVE drops. Software inventory is the input that drives almost every other surface in MDVM. If a piece of software isn’t in the inventory, it can’t be assessed. So one of the first things to check on a new deployment is: does the inventory match reality? Pick five known-installed apps, search for them, confirm the version numbers are right.
What software inventory doesn’t capture out of the box: command-line tools installed via package managers without going through the OS installer registry on Linux, some niche Windows installers that don’t write to the standard registry keys, and side-by-side installations that share an executable name. For 95% of business software, you’re fine. For the other 5%, authenticated scan or a custom approach is the answer.
The premium discovery surfaces (Add-on) If you have the Vulnerability Management Add-on, four extra surfaces light up. These are the ones I see organizations massively under-use.
Browser extensions The portal enumerates every browser extension installed in Edge and Chrome across your fleet, with the publisher, version, permissions requested, and a risk rating. Browser extensions are a chronically overlooked attack surface, someone installs a “cute weather extension” with read-and-write access to all sites, and three months later it gets sold to a different developer who pushes a malicious update. The Add-on lights this whole world up.
Digital certificates Every certificate installed on every endpoint, with expiration date, issuer, key length, and signature algorithm. The first time you turn this on you’ll find at least one of the following: SHA-1 certificates still in production, certificates that expired six months ago and nobody noticed, or self-signed root CAs you never approved. I haven’t run this assessment on a customer environment yet without finding something embarrassing in the first hour.
Network share configuration assessment For every SMB share visible to managed endpoints, MDVM evaluates the permissions: anonymous access, Everyone full control, weak SMB versions enabled, missing signing. This is your “lateral-movement-via-shares” map. For organizations that grew the share structure organically over a decade, the first scan is humbling.
Hardware and firmware BIOS/UEFI versions, processor model, vendor firmware, and known firmware-level CVEs. Niche but valuable, firmware-level vulnerabilities tend to live for years because nobody patches them, and they’re invisible to OS-level scanners. If you’re chasing supply-chain hardware risks (and after the LogoFAIL family of issues, you should be), this is your dashboard.
Authenticated scan: what it is and when to use it Some devices can’t run the MDE sensor. Aging Linux boxes, network appliances, dev test machines that aren’t in scope for endpoint management. For these, MDVM offers authenticated scan, a credentialed network scan from a designated host into the unmanaged target.
Two flavors:
Authenticated Scan for Windows. A Windows-onboarded device in your environment acts as the scanner. You provide a service account with sufficient privileges on the target, and MDVM uses RPC/SMB to enumerate installed software and configuration state on the unmanaged Windows host. You get back the same vulnerability assessment you’d get from an onboarded device, minus the EDR side.
Authenticated Scan for Linux. Same model, but SSH-based, with a credential set you provision in the portal. Supports the major distributions.
When to reach for authenticated scan:
A legacy server that can’t take the MDE sensor (kernel too old, vendor support contract that prohibits agents). A device temporarily out of scope for full management but in scope for assessment. Pre-onboarding due-diligence, you can scan a target before you onboard it, get a baseline, then track what onboarding changes. When not to use it:
As a replacement for full onboarding. Authenticated scan gives you VA but not EDR. If the device matters enough to scan, it usually matters enough to onboard. In OT environments without explicit change-management approval. SSH into a PLC-adjacent device is still a network event, and OT teams have opinions about that. Network device discovery Switches, routers, firewalls, WLAN controllers, the network gear itself. MDVM discovers these through a designated assessment device: a Windows host you nominate (typically near the network gear) that runs SNMP-based discovery and assessment against a list of network targets you provide.
Setup is straightforward but has a few footguns:
The assessment device needs SNMPv3 credentials with read access to each target. SNMPv1/v2 work but are deprecated and you shouldn’t be running them in 2026. The assessment device needs network reachability to each target. In segmented networks this often means coordinating with the network team to allow the assessment device to reach management VLANs. The list of supported vendors is wider than people expect (Cisco, Juniper, Aruba, Fortinet, Palo Alto, F5, and more) but check the current Microsoft docs because it grows. The output: every discovered network device shows up in the device inventory with firmware version and known CVEs, just like an endpoint. For a flour mill with industrial switches, this is genuinely useful.
How fresh is the data? A question I get a lot. Three different cadences:
Software inventory and CVE assessment for a managed endpoint: typically within hours of a change. The MDE sensor reports the change, the cloud re-evaluates, the portal updates.
Configuration assessment: similar, with some recommendations evaluated more frequently than others.
Authenticated scans: on the schedule you set. Default is daily. You can run on-demand for a specific target.
Network device discovery: per the designated assessment device’s schedule.
The headline number: MDVM data is hours old, not days old. That matters when a CVE drops. A traditional scanner running weekly tells you “we are vulnerable” three days after the threat actors started exploiting. MDVM tells you the morning the patch ships, before you’ve had your coffee.
A real-world workflow Let me show you what discovery looks like end-to-end on a typical first MDVM rollout.
Day 1. Onboard your top tier of endpoints to MDE. Check the device inventory. Verify count matches your CMDB.
Day 2. Open Software inventory. Pick the top five vendors by install count. Spot-check that the products and versions are accurate. If anything’s wildly off, your sensor coverage has a gap, fix it now.
Day 3. Turn on passive discovery (or confirm it’s on). Watch the unmanaged device list populate over 48 hours.
Day 5. Triage the unmanaged list. For each device, decide: onboard, authenticated scan, or exclude. Document the decision. (Auditors love this document. NIS2 specifically loves this document.)
Day 7. Stand up the network device assessment box. Add your switches, routers, firewalls.
Day 10. Enable Add-on premium surfaces if licensed. Spend a real hour each on browser extensions, certificates, and network shares. Pick one finding from each and remediate it. This builds team muscle memory more than any documentation will.
After two weeks, you’ve moved from “I think we have visibility” to “I can produce a defensible inventory in five minutes.” That’s the foundation Part 3 needs.
Where to next In Part 3 we get into the prioritization engine, the part of MDVM that earns the “threat-aware” label. Exposure Score, threat insights, breach insights, and the logic that decides which of your 40,000 CVEs to chase first.

Why this one is my personal favourite I said in Part 2 of the Defender Demystified series that Microsoft Defender for Identity is the workload I find most interesting. That’s because it catches what the other three can’t: what an attacker does after they already have valid credentials.
An attacker who phishes a password, buys one from an infostealer marketplace, or dumps it from a compromised laptop now holds a valid identity. From that point, endpoint and email tools have very little to say — the attacker is behaving as a legitimate user. Microsoft Defender for Identity is the one workload that notices.
This post is the practical walkthrough: what the sensors do, how to install them, how the Microsoft Entra ID integration works, and the alerts worth your attention in the first week.
What Microsoft Defender for Identity actually monitors Three sources of identity telemetry:
On-premises Active Directory — authentication traffic, LDAP queries, sensitive group changes, Kerberos activity Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) — if you use it, which most mid-market organisations still do Microsoft Entra ID — hybrid identity signals, risky sign-ins, and (as of recent updates) native tenant integration without a separate sensor Microsoft Defender for Identity correlates these into a single identity-centric view per user: “here’s everything happening with this account, across on-prem and cloud”. That single-view capability is the whole reason the product exists.
What the sensors do, in one paragraph The Microsoft Defender for Identity sensor is a lightweight Windows service you install on domain controllers and AD FS servers. It captures network traffic and event logs from the host it’s running on, parses them for identity-relevant signals, and forwards the relevant metadata to the Microsoft Defender for Identity cloud service. The sensor is designed to run quietly — Microsoft engineered it to use minimal resources on production DCs, which matters because domain controllers are not servers you want to load.
The deployment flow, at a high level 📷 Image 1 — Microsoft Defender for Identity workspace creation. Capture from: Defender portal → Settings → Identities → General. Show the instance / workspace details or the “Create your workspace” flow if you haven’t set it up yet.
The sequence is:
Create your Microsoft Defender for Identity workspace in the Defender portal. This happens automatically the first time you enable the workload. Create a Directory Service account — a specifically-scoped gMSA or service account that the sensor uses to read AD information. Microsoft provides a step-by-step guide for gMSA setup. Download the sensor installer from the Defender portal. Same installer for all sensor types. Install on each domain controller and AD FS server you want to protect. Start with a pilot DC, confirm telemetry flows, then expand. Verify health in the portal under Settings → Identities → Sensors. 📷 Image 2 — Sensor health page after deployment. Capture from: Defender portal → Settings → Identities → Sensors. Show the list of installed sensors with health status green.
Practical tip: install sensors on all your domain controllers, not just a subset. A sensor only sees traffic on the DC it’s installed on — if you skip DCs, the attacks that land there are invisible. The licensing is per-user, not per-sensor, so there’s no cost reason to skip any.
The Microsoft Entra ID piece Recent updates to Microsoft Defender for Identity added direct Microsoft Entra ID integration — the product now ingests Microsoft Entra ID signals (risky sign-ins, impossible travel, suspicious token activity) natively into the same unified identity timeline it builds for on-prem AD.
📷 Image 3 — Unified identity view in the Defender portal. Capture from: Defender portal → Assets → Identities → open any user. Show the identity overview combining on-prem AD and Entra ID signals. Redact user name.
The result: you get one view per user that spans both on-prem and cloud identity. This is genuinely useful. Before the integration, analysts had to pivot between Defender for Identity (for on-prem signals) and Microsoft Entra ID Protection (for cloud signals). Now a single incident correlates across both surfaces.
What alerts to expect in the first week Microsoft Defender for Identity ships with over 50 built-in detections across four attack phases:
Reconnaissance — an attacker scoping your environment:
Account enumeration LDAP reconnaissance Network mapping reconnaissance via DNS Security principal reconnaissance Compromised credentials — an attacker using stolen credentials:
Suspected brute-force attack Suspected AS-REP roasting Honey-token account authentication Lateral movement — an attacker moving through your network:
Suspected pass-the-hash attack Suspected pass-the-ticket attack Suspected overpass-the-hash attack Remote code execution attempt Domain dominance — an attacker consolidating control:
Suspected Golden Ticket usage Suspected DCSync attack Suspected skeleton key attack Suspicious modification of sensitive groups 📷 Image 4 — Active alerts view in the Identities section. Capture from: Defender portal → Incidents & alerts → Alerts, filtered for “Identity” source, OR from the Identity-specific alerts view in Settings → Identities. Show a list of recent alerts. Redact user names.
The honest guidance: expect a few low-confidence alerts in the first week, most of them benign — things like penetration testers on a scheduled assessment, legitimate admin tooling that looks like reconnaissance, and service accounts doing LDAP queries that look weird out of context. Tune the exclusions, don’t disable the alerts. Microsoft provides built-in exclusion mechanisms for each detection so you can whitelist the specific accounts or hosts that cause benign noise.
The settings worth configuring Directory Service account — as noted, scoped correctly from the start. Don’t use Domain Admin; use the documented least-privilege gMSA.
Sensitive accounts list — under Settings → Identities → Sensitive groups, configure which accounts and groups Microsoft Defender for Identity should treat as extra-valuable. Domain Admins are there by default; add your Tier 0 service accounts, backup operators, and any custom admin groups you maintain.
📷 Image 5 — Sensitive accounts configuration. Capture from: Defender portal → Settings → Identities → Sensitive groups. Show the configured sensitive groups.
Honey-token accounts — Microsoft Defender for Identity supports configuring decoy accounts that should never be authenticated with. Any attempt to authenticate triggers a high-confidence alert. I like these — they’re genuinely useful signals and the configuration overhead is minimal.
Response actions — for customers on the right Microsoft Entra ID tier, Microsoft Defender for Identity can trigger automated account disablement or force password reset on confirmed malicious activity. Enable this carefully and in staged mode first.
A reasonable first-month plan Week 1 — Install sensors on a pilot DC pair, verify telemetry, confirm Microsoft Entra ID integration is active. Week 2 — Expand sensors to all remaining DCs and AD FS servers. Configure the gMSA correctly. Week 3 — Configure sensitive accounts list, deploy honey-token accounts, review the first batch of alerts. Week 4 — Tune exclusions for benign noise, enable staged response actions, schedule a monthly alert review. Where to go from here 🔗 Read the rest of the Microsoft Defender Up Close series: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps.

⚠️ Prices move. Everything below is in USD, list price, as of July 1, 2026, when Microsoft’s most recent pricing and packaging update took effect. Local pricing varies by region and currency. Always double-check on the official Microsoft 365 plans page and the Microsoft Defender for Cloud pricing page before making a purchase decision.
The licensing conversation most of us dread If you’ve done any time in Microsoft security, you’ll have had this meeting. Finance or procurement wants a number. Leadership wants to know whether you’re over-licensed or under-licensed. Someone says “let’s just buy E5, problem solved” and someone else says “E5 is overkill, we’re a small shop”. A third person mentions the “Defender Suite” that they heard about at a conference but nobody in the room is entirely sure what that includes.
Everyone wants clarity. Nobody wants to read the Microsoft 365 Subscription Suites licensing guidance end to end, which is fair, it’s thorough and important but it isn’t exactly written to help you make a Tuesday-morning decision.
This post is the Tuesday-morning version. We’ll cover what Microsoft 365 Business Premium, E3, and E5 actually give you from the Defender family, the newish Defender Suite add-ons that Microsoft launched in late 2025, three realistic organisation profiles, and a decision flow you can take into your next budget meeting.
Two universes to keep separate in your head Before we look at any plan comparison, this distinction:
Microsoft Defender XDR (everything we covered in Part 2, endpoint, email, identity, SaaS) is licensed per user, per month as part of a Microsoft 365 plan. Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Part 3 — Azure and multicloud workloads) is licensed per resource, per month as part of your Azure consumption. These show up on different invoices. Your Microsoft 365 E5 license gives you zero Microsoft Defender for Cloud entitlement, and vice versa. I’ve seen companies budget for “Defender” as a single line item and be unpleasantly surprised when the two different products turn up as two different costs.
The rest of this post focuses on the per-user, Microsoft 365 side. We’ll close with a quick note on the Azure side.
The Microsoft 365 ladder, from least to most security 📷 Image 1: Which Defender products come with which Microsoft 365 plan.
Here’s what each main Microsoft 365 plan currently includes from the Defender family, after the July 2026 packaging update that added meaningful security capabilities to lower-tier plans.
Microsoft 365 Business Basic: $7/user/month Safe Links URL checks in Outlook (added in the 2026 packaging update) That’s it from the Defender family. This plan is for lightweight collaboration accounts that barely need security tooling.
Microsoft 365 Business Standard: $14/user/month Safe Links URL checks in Outlook Similar story. Business Standard is a productivity plan, not a security plan.
Microsoft 365 Business Premium: $22/user/month This is the security sweet spot for anyone under 300 users. Worth flagging that its price did not change in the July 2026 update while E3 and E5 both went up, so the value gap has actually widened. What you get:
Microsoft Defender for Business: a streamlined Microsoft Defender for Endpoint experience with simpler setup and SMB-friendly defaults Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 1: Safe Links, Safe Attachments, anti-phishing Microsoft Entra ID P1: Conditional Access, MFA enforcement Microsoft Intune Plan 1: full mobile device and application management For a small or mid-sized business, one $22 license replaces what used to need a separate antivirus, an email security gateway, an MDM product, and an identity governance tool. The only real ceiling is the 300-user cap, once you cross that, you need to move to Enterprise plans.
Honestly, if someone asks me the single best per-dollar security decision in the entire Microsoft catalogue, this is my answer. It’s not close.
Microsoft 365 E3: $39/user/month E3 is the standard enterprise productivity plan. After the July 2026 packaging update, it includes noticeably more security than it used to:
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 1: preventive endpoint protection Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 1: (newly added in 2026), Safe Links, Safe Attachments, anti-phishing Microsoft Entra ID P1: Conditional Access, MFA, basic identity governance Microsoft Intune Plan 1 + Plan 2: including Remote Help and Advanced Analytics Windows 11 Enterprise E3 works if you want enterprise productivity plus basic security, with the option to bolt on advanced security separately.
Microsoft 365 E5: $60/user/month E5 is the full enterprise security stack in a single per-user SKU. Everything in E3, plus:
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 2: full EDR, automated investigation and response, vulnerability management Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2: adds Attack Simulation Training and Threat Explorer Microsoft Defender for Identity: on-premises AD and Microsoft Entra ID protection Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps: the CASB for SaaS visibility and control Microsoft Entra ID P2: Privileged Identity Management, Identity Protection Microsoft Sentinel: integration, unified into the Defender portal Microsoft Security Copilot: (newly included at no extra cost in 2026) Microsoft Purview: advanced compliance, eDiscovery Premium, Insider Risk Management Microsoft Cloud PKI: (added in 2026) Microsoft Power BI Pro E5 is for organisations that want a unified security and compliance stack from one vendor rather than stitching together point products. The $21 gap over E3 sounds like a lot until you price out what it would cost you separately for a SIEM, an EDR, a CASB, identity protection, Power BI, and now Security Copilot. Those numbers add up fast.
Microsoft 365 E7: $99/user/month (new in 2026) The new top tier. Everything in E5 plus Microsoft 365 Copilot, Microsoft Entra Suite, and Microsoft Agent 365. This one is for AI-forward enterprises and isn’t primarily a security upgrade, E5 already gives you the full Defender story.
The 2026 Defender Suite add-ons, actually useful flexibility Until late 2025, if you wanted E5-level Defender capabilities but were stuck on E3 or Business Premium, your only realistic option was the full upgrade. That changed. Microsoft launched standalone Defender Suite add-ons that let you layer enterprise-grade security onto lower-tier plans without committing to E5 across the board.
Microsoft Defender Suite: (formerly “Microsoft 365 E5 Security”), adds to Microsoft 365 E3 the missing pieces: Defender for Endpoint Plan 2, Defender for Office 365 Plan 2, Defender for Identity, Defender for Cloud Apps, and Microsoft Entra ID P2. Microsoft Defender Suite for Business Premium: the same idea for Business Premium customers. (Separately, since October 2025, Business Premium is no longer a required prerequisite to purchase the standard Defender Suite add-on on top of E3.) One small but important operational note from the Microsoft licensing docs: a tenant that ends up with both Microsoft Defender for Business (from Business Premium) and Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 (from the Defender Suite add-on) defaults to the Defender for Business experience. Plan accordingly if you’re mixing.
📷 Image 2: Official Microsoft 365 Business pricing, plain tier vs Copilot-bundled tier.
Three realistic scenarios Scenario 1: the small firm (50 people) Profile: 50 knowledge workers, no on-premises infrastructure, hybrid work, GDPR obligations, no dedicated security team.
Recommendation: Microsoft 365 Business Premium. That’s the whole answer.
For around $1,100 a month total, you get genuinely strong security, endpoint protection, email protection, Conditional Access, MFA, MDM. You won’t outgrow it until you hit 300 users. For any professional asked to secure a small firm on a realistic budget, this is the cleanest recommendation you can make.
If you also handle highly sensitive data (legal, healthcare, financial advisory), consider adding the Microsoft Defender Suite for Business Premium add-on. You get the full enterprise Defender stack at SMB-friendly pricing.
Scenario 2: the mid-market organisation (500 people) Profile: 500 people, a mix of office and shop-floor workers, on-premises Active Directory, growing Microsoft Entra ID footprint, ISO 27001 in scope, NIS2 in scope, a small but real security team.
Recommendation: Microsoft 365 E3 + Microsoft Defender Suite add-on for the office workers, Microsoft 365 F3 for the shop-floor workers.
Why this beats standardising on E5:
Shop-floor users (say 200 of the 500) don’t need full E3 or E5. F3 at $10/user/month is the right fit. The 300 office knowledge workers get E3 ($39) plus the Defender Suite add-on, which gives them E5-equivalent security at a lower blended cost than E5 across the board. If you don’t have 24x7 SOC coverage in-house, the Microsoft Defender Experts Suite (generally available from January 2026) layers managed XDR services on top. This pattern (right-sizing licenses instead of uniformly deploying E5) saves mid-market organisations 15–30% in many engagements I’ve seen. It’s worth the thirty minutes to actually do the analysis.
Scenario 3: the enterprise (5,000 people, multicloud) Profile: 5,000 people, multiple business units, hybrid AD plus Microsoft Entra ID, full SOC team, compliance obligations spanning ISO 27001, NIS2, GDPR, and DORA, workloads running in both Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services.
Recommendation: a tiered mix:
E5 for executives, legal, finance, IT, and the security team (roughly 5–10% of users) to unlock Privileged Identity Management, Microsoft Security Copilot, eDiscovery Premium E3 + Defender Suite add-on for the majority (~80%) of standard knowledge workers F1 / F3 for frontline workers Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans (Defender CSPM plus Defender for Servers Plan 2 plus Defender for Storage, and others as needed) on the Azure side Microsoft Sentinel as the SIEM, unified into the Defender portal The mistake a lot of enterprises make is uniform E5 deployment without actually checking feature usage. Industry data suggests around 38% of E5 licenses are oversized for their actual users. That’s a real recovery opportunity whenever someone does the analysis properly.
What about Microsoft Defender for Cloud pricing? Quick recap from Part 3:
Foundational CSPM: free for any onboarded Azure subscription, AWS account, or GCP project Defender CSPM: (paid tier) around $5 per billable resource per month CWPP plans: (Servers, Storage, Containers, Databases, and the rest) each with its own per-resource pricing Use the official calculator before enabling. Costs scale with your estate, and large estates can add up quickly.
A decision flow you can actually use If you take one thing from this post, take this:
Under 300 users, no special compliance burden? → Microsoft 365 Business Premium Under 300 users, regulated industry or sensitive data? → Business Premium + Defender Suite for Business Premium add-on 300+ users, basic security needs, flexibility valued? → E3 + Defender Suite add-on for security-tier users 300+ users, want everything in one SKU? → E5 (but right-size — don’t deploy uniformly) Frontline workers in any of the above? → F1 / F3 + appropriate F-series security add-ons Any Azure / AWS / GCP workloads? → Foundational CSPM turned on today (free), then evaluate paid plans 📷 Image 3a: Under 300 users: choosing between Business Premium and Business Premium + Defender Suite.
📷 Image 3b: 300+ users: choosing between E3 + Defender Suite and right-sized E5.
Frontline workers in either scenario → F1/F3 + appropriate add-ons. Azure/AWS/GCP workloads → enable the free Foundational CSPM today, then evaluate paid plans.
What’s next In Part 5, the final post of this series, we open the Microsoft Defender portal at security.microsoft.com together and go on a guided tour. Where to find each workload, where Microsoft Secure Score now lives, how to set up the right roles, and a practical “first hour in the portal” agenda you can follow today.

Welcome to Part 3. This is the part of MDVM that maps directly to the 4-hour problem from the bridge post, and the part most people under-use the most. Discovery (Part 2) tells you what’s there. Remediation (Part 4) tells you what to do about it. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management prioritization is the brain in the middle that decides what’s worth doing right now and what can wait.
If you walk away from this series with one habit, make it this: stop reading CVE lists sorted by CVSS. You’ll burn out, you’ll fix the wrong things first, and the things that actually get exploited will live in your environment unfixed because they had a CVSS of 7.4 and you were chasing the 9.8s that nobody’s actually using.
MDVM gives you a better signal. Let’s break it down.
The math problem you can’t win The National Vulnerability Database publishes roughly 40,000 to 50,000 new CVEs per year as of 2025. The average enterprise has tens of thousands of “vulnerabilities” present in its environment at any given moment when measured by the traditional “CVE × asset” formula. Most of those are duplicates of the same underlying issue, but even after deduplication you’re staring at thousands.
You cannot fix thousands. You don’t have the change windows, the testing capacity, or the patience.
The good news is you don’t have to. Of all those CVEs, the percentage that are actively being exploited in the wild at any given moment is a fraction of a fraction. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) maintains the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog (currently over 1,200 entries) and that’s the entire universe of vulnerabilities they’ve confirmed are being used by attackers. EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) data tells a similar story: only a small percentage of CVEs ever get exploited.
Your job isn’t to fix every vulnerability. Your job is to fix the ones that are likely to be used against you, in your environment, before the attacker gets to them. MDVM’s prioritization engine exists to help you make that call.
Exposure Score The headline number in MDVM is Exposure Score, displayed prominently in the Vulnerability management dashboard. It’s a number between 0 and 100, where lower is better. (Yes, this is the opposite of Microsoft Secure Score, where higher is better. I know. I’ve complained.)
Exposure Score represents your tenant-wide vulnerability and weakness posture, weighted by:
The severity of vulnerabilities present The exploitability of those vulnerabilities (active exploits, kits, public POCs) The device value (high-value devices weighted more heavily) The number of devices affected It’s deliberately a single number, because executive dashboards demand single numbers. Underneath it is a richer breakdown, by device, by software, by vulnerability, that you’ll spend most of your time in.
The trap to avoid: treating Exposure Score as a goal in itself. It’s a thermometer, not a treatment plan. Driving it from 78 to 65 in a quarter is a real outcome. Driving it from 78 to 65 by silencing recommendations or excluding devices is theatre. I’ve seen both.
Microsoft Secure Score for Devices (different thing) Right alongside Exposure Score, MDVM displays Microsoft Secure Score for Devices, also 0–100, where higher is better. They sound the same. They are not the same.
Exposure Score: vulnerability- and threat-driven. “How exposed am I to attack?” Secure Score for Devices: configuration-driven. “How well are my devices configured against an established hardening baseline?” Secure Score for Devices maps to the same hardening recommendations Microsoft publishes for Windows, macOS, and Linux: things like “ensure SMB signing is required,” “enable BitLocker,” “disable unnecessary services.” Each control is worth points. Implement the control across your fleet, your score goes up.
Both scores matter. Exposure Score answers “am I likely to get hit.” Secure Score for Devices answers “is the hit likely to succeed.” Mature programs watch both.
And, for those of you reading the Secure Score as Cyber GRC series, these device-level scores feed the tenant-wide Microsoft Secure Score in the broader portal. We’ll close that loop in Part 4.
Threat Insights, the heart of “threat-aware” Now we get to the part that earns MDVM the “threat-aware” label. Every vulnerability in MDVM is decorated with Threat Insights, small icons next to the CVE that tell you what’s actually happening with that vulnerability in the real world.
The signals to know:
Exploit available. A working exploit exists somewhere, a public POC, a Metasploit module, exploit kit code. The vulnerability has crossed from “theoretical” to “executable.”
Exploit verified. Microsoft has confirmed the exploit works against the affected configuration. Not just “someone published code” but “we’ve seen it function.” Higher confidence than Exploit available.
Exploit in kit. The exploit is bundled into a commercial or commodity exploit kit, meaning every script kiddie now has access to it, not just sophisticated actors. This is when the volume goes through the roof.
Linked to active threat campaign. Microsoft’s threat intelligence has tied the vulnerability to a named campaign or actor that’s currently active. Translation: someone is actively using this against organizations like yours, right now.
High-profile threat. Microsoft has designated the vulnerability as part of a high-profile threat, typically when there’s broad active exploitation across many sectors.
These signals are not theory. They’re not estimated. They’re observed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence teams across a planetary-scale telemetry base. When MDVM tells you a CVE is “linked to active threat campaign,” that’s not a hypothesis, it’s a current fact.
The right way to use Threat Insights: filter the recommendations list by the presence of these signals, and start there. A CVE with all five signals lit and a CVSS of 7.4 is a far higher priority than a CVE with no signals and a CVSS of 9.8. The second one is theoretical. The first one is being used to break into someone’s environment as you read this.
Breach Insights A different signal, equally important. Breach Insights flags vulnerabilities on devices where Defender for Endpoint has already raised an alert. The interpretation is direct, there’s smoke on this device, and a known vulnerability could be the fire. Whether or not the alert and the vulnerability are causally connected, a device with both is more likely to be in trouble than a device with either alone.
I keep a saved query that lists every device with both an active alert and a Critical/High CVE present. That list is short and it’s the list I look at first, every day.
Asset Value and Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Device-Level Prioritization A CVE on the laptop of an intern matters less than the same CVE on the domain controller. MDVM lets you mark devices by value (High, Normal, Low) and the prioritization engine weights findings accordingly. A High-value device with a moderately exploitable vulnerability outranks a Low-value device with a severely exploitable one.
The standard practice I recommend:
High value: domain controllers, certificate authorities, identity servers, backup infrastructure, jump hosts, OT supervisor workstations, any host holding regulated data. Normal value: standard endpoints and servers. Low value: lab and test devices, throwaway VMs. Tagging takes an afternoon. The payoff lasts for the life of the tenant. Don’t skip it.
Threat Analytics, the briefing for what you should care about today Adjacent to MDVM, in Defender XDR, is Threat Analytics, a feed of analyst-written reports on currently active threats: ransomware campaigns, vulnerability exploitation waves, threat actor profiles. Each report includes:
A description of the threat The IOCs and TTPs being observed The Microsoft mitigations that apply And , critically, a list of the vulnerabilities exploited in the campaign, with direct links to the corresponding MDVM recommendations This is the loop that closes 4 hours into something you can act on. A new campaign drops. The Threat Analytics report appears. You click through to the linked vulnerability. MDVM tells you exactly which devices in your tenant have it. You request remediation in Intune. End-to-end response in minutes, not days.
Most organizations I see have never opened Threat Analytics. It is the single highest-ROI surface in the entire Defender XDR portal, and it’s there with the Core licensing.
Zero-day handling The 4-hour problem includes vulnerabilities that don’t have CVE numbers yet. How does MDVM handle those?
Two paths.
The behavioral path. Defender for Endpoint’s EDR side detects the exploitation behavior, process injection, suspicious API calls, anomalous payloads — even when the vulnerability itself isn’t catalogued. This is EDR doing its job; MDVM doesn’t claim to detect zero-days at the vulnerability layer.
The fast-update path. Once a zero-day becomes a known-exploited-vulnerability (typically within hours of the first observed attack) Microsoft pushes an update to the MDVM signature feed. Your tenant gets the new CVE the moment it’s catalogued, with Threat Insights already populated based on the early observations. There’s no scanner-update cycle to wait through.
The honest framing: MDVM doesn’t predict zero-days. Nobody does. What MDVM does is collapse the time between “this is now a public threat” and “I know which of my devices are exposed” to near-zero. Combined with EDR-side behavioral detection, that’s the best the industry currently offers.
A Real Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Prioritization Workflow This is what a Tuesday-morning routine looks like with MDVM doing the heavy lifting:
Step 1. Open the Vulnerability management dashboard. Glance at Exposure Score and Secure Score for Devices. Are they where they were yesterday? If something jumped, why?
Step 2. Open Recommendations, sort by Exposure Score impact, filter by Threat Insights = “linked to active threat campaign” OR “exploit verified.”
Step 3. For each recommendation in that filtered list, open it. Read the affected device count, the affected software, the linked threats. Decide: request remediation, accept the risk with documented justification, or escalate.
Step 4. Open Threat Analytics. Are there new high-relevance reports since yesterday? If yes, click into each one and check whether the linked vulnerabilities affect your tenant.
Step 5. Run your Breach Insights saved query. Any device with both an active alert and a high-severity CVE, investigate now.
That whole flow is 20 to 30 minutes. It is not theoretical — it’s what a working SOC analyst does daily once the muscle memory builds. And it’s the operational answer to the 4-hour problem: by the time the attacker is ready to exploit, you’ve already triaged what’s exposed and queued the remediation.
Where to next We’ve identified what to fix. Part 4 is about actually fixing it, Intune one-click remediation, ServiceNow ticketing, Security Baselines, blocking vulnerable applications, and the integration story across Sentinel, Advanced Hunting, and the wider Microsoft Secure Score.

Why CASBs exist at all A CASB — Cloud Access Security Broker — exists because the way people work changed faster than traditional security tools could adapt. Fifteen years ago, your security stack sat between your users and a small number of applications you’d sanctioned. Now your users authenticate to dozens of cloud services daily, many of which your IT team never explicitly approved.
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps is Microsoft’s answer to this problem. It gives you visibility into what cloud apps your users are actually using, governance over the OAuth consents and file sharing happening in those apps, and threat protection against the anomalous user behaviour that signals a compromised account.
This post is the practical follow-up to Part 2 of the Defender Demystified series. Four main capabilities, one at a time.
Capability 1 — Shadow IT discovery The single most eye-opening capability when you first enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps is Shadow IT discovery. The product ingests logs from your network edge (firewalls, web proxies) or from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (which already sees all your devices’ web traffic), correlates them against a catalogue of over 31,000 cloud apps, and produces a dashboard of what your users are actually using.
📷 Image 1 — Cloud app catalog / discovered apps dashboard. Capture from: Defender portal → Cloud apps → Cloud Discovery → Discovered apps. Show the app list with risk scores, usage counts, and traffic volume. Redact sensitive app names if needed.
What you’ll find, essentially always:
More apps than you thought — typically 3–5x the number your IT team believed existed A long tail of low-usage apps (marketing tools, file converters, random SaaS one person signed up for) A handful of genuinely risky apps you need to deal with (unsanctioned file-sharing, unmanaged storage, non-compliant AI tools) Each app in the catalogue has a risk score (0–10) calculated from roughly 90 risk factors — data encryption at rest, GDPR compliance, SOC 2 certification, data retention policies, supports SSO, supports SAML, and so on. You can customise the scoring weights if your organisation has specific priorities.
The easiest way to enable discovery is through the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration — if you already have Defender for Endpoint deployed, discovery works automatically without any extra configuration on your network side.
📷 Image 2 — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration toggle. Capture from: Defender portal → Settings → Cloud apps → Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. Show the integration toggle and status.
What to do with the discovery output: work through the top 20 unsanctioned apps by usage, decide which to sanction (mark as approved), unsanction (mark as not approved — which can trigger blocking through Defender for Endpoint), or investigate further. This is an ongoing exercise, not a one-time cleanup.
Capability 2 — OAuth app governance This one is underrated. When a user grants an OAuth application permission to access their Microsoft 365 data — say, a calendar scheduling app that wants to read and write their calendar — that grant persists, invisibly, until explicitly revoked. If the user was phished into granting consent to a malicious app, the attacker now has ongoing access to mail or files without ever having stolen a password.
App governance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps gives you visibility and control over every OAuth grant in your tenant.
📷 Image 3 — OAuth apps overview. Capture from: Defender portal → Cloud apps → OAuth apps. Show the list of consented apps with publisher, permissions, user count, and any risk flags. Redact sensitive app names.
What to look for:
Apps requesting high-privilege permissions — anything asking for Mail.ReadWrite, Files.ReadWrite.All, or Directory.Read.All without an obvious business reason Apps from unknown publishers — legitimate vendors generally have verified publisher status Apps with low user counts in your tenant but broad permissions — a single user with a high-risk app is a common phishing outcome Apps flagged by Microsoft threat intelligence — the portal marks these directly Microsoft publishes detection policies for OAuth abuse (e.g., “suspicious consent pattern”, “misleading OAuth app name”). Review the flagged apps weekly and revoke consent on anything suspicious — the portal offers one-click revocation across all users who granted consent to an app.
Capability 3 — Conditional Access App Control Conditional Access App Control is the session-level policy engine. It integrates with Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access to apply real-time session controls to risky sessions — not just “block or allow” at sign-in, but “allow, but restrict what the user can do once they’re in”.
Example policies you can build:
“Users on unmanaged devices can read SharePoint documents in the browser but cannot download them” “Users outside corporate network can access Salesforce but cannot print or copy records” “Users flagged as high-risk can authenticate to Microsoft 365 but every session activity is logged for review” 📷 Image 4 — Conditional Access App Control session policy configuration. Capture from: Defender portal → Cloud apps → Policies → Session policy. Show a policy creation view with the session control options visible.
The setup takes some planning — you need the right Conditional Access policy in Microsoft Entra ID pointing traffic through Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, plus the session policy in Defender for Cloud Apps itself. Microsoft’s deployment guide walks through the full flow.
One high-value use case to start with: block downloads from unmanaged devices for your most sensitive SharePoint sites. It’s genuinely effective at stopping data exfiltration, and it doesn’t affect anyone using a managed device.
Capability 4 — Activity and file policies The final layer is activity policies and file policies — detection rules that fire on user behaviour or file content across all your connected cloud apps.
Activity policy examples:
Impossible travel (sign-in from Athens and New York within an hour) Mass download (a single user downloads 1,000+ files in an hour) Suspicious inbox forwarding rules (a classic BEC signal) Admin activity from a non-admin account File policy examples:
A file containing a regex-matched pattern (credit card number, IBAN, passport number) shared externally A SharePoint document labelled “Confidential” moved to a OneDrive folder that’s shared with anonymous link 📷 Image 5 — Policies overview page. Capture from: Defender portal → Cloud apps → Policies → Policy management. Show the list of configured activity and file policies.
Microsoft ships a set of default anomaly detection policies that are already enabled out of the box — impossible travel, ransomware activity, mass delete, suspicious inbox forwarding. Don’t re-invent these; just review them and make sure the alert destinations are correct.
For file policies, start by connecting Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels (if you use them) and building one simple policy — “any file labelled Confidential shared externally triggers an alert”. That one policy delivers disproportionate value.
A reasonable first-month plan Week 1 — Enable the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration for Cloud Discovery. Let it collect data. Don’t act yet. Week 2 — Review the discovered apps dashboard. Sanction your top 20 known good apps; unsanction the clearly risky ones. Review top-risk OAuth apps and revoke any with no business justification. Week 3 — Enable the default anomaly detection policies (most are on by default; verify). Configure one custom file policy for sensitive content. Week 4 — Plan and pilot Conditional Access App Control for one use case (e.g., block SharePoint downloads from unmanaged devices for a pilot group). By the end of month one you have a working CASB, real visibility into your SaaS estate, and the OAuth and session controls that most organisations never get around to implementing.
Where to go from here 🔗 Read the rest of the Microsoft Defender Up Close series: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender for Identity.

We’ve reached the end Over four posts we’ve built up the full picture of the Microsoft Defender family:
Part 1 — the whole family the way Microsoft itself organises it Part 2 — the four core XDR workloads Part 3 — Microsoft Defender for Cloud for Azure and multicloud Part 4 — which plan to actually buy Time to open the platform itself. This final post is a hands-on walk through the unified Microsoft Defender portal at security.microsoft.com, the single console where everything we’ve covered lives. Open the portal in another tab and read along. By the end, you’ll know where everything is and what to click first.
📷 Image 1: The Microsoft Defender portal home page, your dashboard for incidents, Microsoft Secure Score, and threat analytics.
The portal in one sentence The Microsoft Defender portal brings together Microsoft Defender XDR (endpoint, email, identity, SaaS), Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Azure and multicloud workloads), Microsoft Sentinel (SIEM), Microsoft Security Exposure Management (posture and Secure Score), and Microsoft Security Copilot (AI assistance) into a single navigation experience. What any given tenant actually sees depends on what’s licensed, Microsoft only renders the sections your subscription includes.
As of 2026, Microsoft Sentinel is generally available inside the Defender portal, and the standalone Sentinel experience in the Azure portal retires on 31 March 2027, a date Microsoft extended from the originally announced 1 July 2026 following customer feedback. If you’re still bouncing between the Azure portal and security.microsoft.com, you’re working harder than you need to.
Walking the left navigation, top to bottom The left navigation is the map. Each major section, in the order you’ll see it.
Home 📷 Image 2a: The Microsoft Defender portal left navigation, upper section, from Home through Threat intelligence.
📷 Image 2b: The Microsoft Defender portal left navigation, lower section, from Assets through System settings.
The Home page is your dashboard, active incidents, recent alerts, Microsoft Secure Score trend, highlighted threat analytics reports, and (for customers with Microsoft Defender Experts for XDR) a service status card. Customise cards with Add cards in the top-right to match your role.
For a security manager or IT leader, this is your morning-coffee page. For a SOC analyst, you’ll spend more time further down in Investigation & response.
Exposure management, where Microsoft Secure Score now lives This is the section most people overlook because the branding is relatively new for what used to be a scattered set of features. Microsoft Security Exposure Management is Microsoft’s unified posture surface, your overall exposure score, attack surface, critical asset coverage, and a few things worth calling out by name:
Microsoft Secure Score: moved here from its previous home, now sitting alongside the broader exposure picture Recommendations prioritised by risk, not just by configuration drift Attack paths: predictive analysis of how an attacker could actually move through your environment If you’ve read How We Built a Gold-Winning GRC Programme on Microsoft Secure Score, this section is where that entire programme lives. The Microsoft Secure Score data feed that powers the compliance pipeline comes straight from this page.
📷 Image 3: Microsoft Secure Score now lives under Exposure management, score, trend, and prioritised recommendations in one page.
Investigation & response — the SOC heart of the portal This is where SOC analysts live. Three subsections:
Incidents & alerts: the unified queue. Every alert from every workload (Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Office 365, Identity, Cloud Apps, Defender for Cloud, Sentinel analytics rules) flows here, automatically grouped into incidents that share entities, timeline, or attack-stage signals. Hunting: proactive search across your telemetry. The flagship feature is Advanced hunting using Kusto Query Language (KQL). Threat analytics: Microsoft-curated threat reports joined to your tenant data, so the second a new threat actor’s TTPs are published you can see whether anything in your environment matches. 📷 Image 4: One queue for every workload, the Service sources column shows which Defender product raised each incident.
A simple KQL query to try as your first run in Advanced hunting, this lists sign-ins from the last 24 hours, grouped by country:
SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | summarize SigninCount = count() by Location | order by SigninCount desc Note that SigninLogs is a Microsoft Sentinel table, it only appears in advanced hunting if you’ve onboarded a Sentinel workspace to the Defender portal. If you have Microsoft Entra ID P2 but no Sentinel workspace, use the native Defender XDR table EntraIdSignInEvents instead (this replaced AADSignInEventsBeta in December 2025). If you have neither, this one runs on Microsoft Defender for Endpoint data alone:
DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, OSVersion, DeviceType) by DeviceId, DeviceName | where isnotempty(OSPlatform) | summarize DeviceCount = count() by OSPlatform, OSVersion, DeviceType | order by DeviceCount desc 📷 Image 5: Advanced hunting with a KQL query loaded, a full device inventory in five lines, using Defender for Endpoint data alone.
Threat intelligence Two main pages here:
Threat analytics (also accessible from Investigation & response) — Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center reports, ranked by relevance to your tenant Intel profiles and explorer (for customers with Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence), threat actor profiles, IOCs, infrastructure tracking For most organisations, the curated threat analytics reports alone are the highest-value content here. Worth a weekly skim.
Assets A unified inventory page, devices, users, mailboxes, applications. Click into any asset for its full risk profile, recent alerts, and entity relationships. This is the page that turns “alert fired on host XYZ” into “this is the CFO’s laptop, here’s everything happening on it, and here are the two other devices they commonly authenticate from”.
Microsoft Sentinel, now native in the portal If you’ve onboarded a Log Analytics workspace with Microsoft Sentinel enabled, Microsoft Sentinel sections appear in the navigation: analytics rules, hunting, workbooks, automation, content hub, data connectors. Microsoft Sentinel in the Defender portal runs the same SIEM you may know from the Azure portal, but federated with Microsoft Defender XDR’s incident model. A single Sentinel rule alert can now correlate with Defender XDR signals into one unified incident.
This integration is one of the more significant Microsoft Security improvements of the last two years, and the reason Microsoft is sunsetting the Azure-portal Sentinel experience. If you’ve been putting off the transition, Part 4 of your 2026 to-do list has arrived.
The four workload sections, Endpoints, Email & collaboration, Identities, Cloud apps These are the per-workload deep-dive panes for the four products we covered in Part 2. Most day-to-day administrative work for each workload happens here:
Endpoints: device inventory, vulnerabilities, software inventory, security baselines, attack surface reduction rules, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint policies Email & collaboration: Threat Explorer, Submissions, Quarantine, Attack simulation training, the anti-phishing/anti-spam/anti-malware policies for Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Identities: identity timelines, sensitive group monitoring, identity security posture, Microsoft Defender for Identity sensor health Cloud apps: discovered cloud apps, app governance, Conditional Access App Control, Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps policies Expect to spend most of your hands-on configuration time inside these four sections.
Cloud security, where Microsoft Defender for Cloud signals now appear Microsoft Defender for Cloud is integrated into the Defender portal. The Cloud security section gives you the cloud overview dashboard, multicloud asset inventory, posture management, and recommendations, without leaving the unified portal. Configuration of Defender for Cloud plans still happens in the Azure portal, but daily operational work (incidents, posture, recommendations) is here now.
SOC optimization Microsoft-generated recommendations that suggest where to tighten your detections, reduce noise, and close coverage gaps, based on your tenant’s actual data ingestion and current posture. Worth fifteen minutes every couple of weeks.
Reports Pre-built reports across every workload. Useful for monthly leadership packs without building dashboards from scratch.
Settings & permissions, the section to set up first 📷 Image 6: The Permissions and roles page. If Microsoft Defender XDR Unified RBAC hasn’t been activated in your tenant yet, this is what you’ll see — a starting point, not an error.
In 2026, Microsoft consolidated permissions into Microsoft Defender XDR Unified RBAC. Three RBAC models now coexist in the portal, and this is genuinely worth understanding before you hand anyone the URL:
Microsoft Entra ID directory roles: broad roles like Security Administrator, Security Reader Workload-specific RBAC: for legacy compatibility (Defender for Endpoint device groups, Defender for Office 365 Exchange-based roles) Microsoft Defender XDR Unified RBAC: the modern model with fine-grained permissions across workloads One thing worth knowing before you go looking for it: Unified RBAC isn’t switched on by default. It has to be activated explicitly, per workload, and until you do that your tenant keeps using Entra ID directory roles and workload-specific RBAC. That activation changes who can see what, so treat it as a planned change with its own testing and comms, not something to click through on a quiet afternoon.
For a team getting started, the practical setup:
Security Administrator for SOC leads who configure policies Security Operator for analysts who investigate and respond Security Reader for auditors, managers, or external read-only access Sort this out before inviting anyone in. I’ve seen the cleanup conversation after the fact and it’s never fun.
Your first hour in the Microsoft Defender portal If you’re opening this portal for the first time today, here’s a productive 60-minute agenda:
Minutes 0–10: Go to Settings → Permissions. Verify the right people have the right roles. Add yourself with Security Administrator if needed. Minutes 10–20: Open Exposure management → Microsoft Secure Score. Look at your overall score and read the top five recommendations. Don’t change anything yet. Just absorb. Minutes 20–35: Visit each of the four workload sections — Endpoints, Email & collaboration, Identities, Cloud apps. Confirm what’s deployed. Note anything that shows “not configured” or empty. Minutes 35–45: Open Investigation & response → Incidents and read three recent incidents end-to-end. This teaches more about what your platform actually sees than any documentation will. Minutes 45–55: Run one of the sample KQL queries from earlier in Advanced hunting. Change the time window. Group by a different field. Get a feel for the editor. Minutes 55–60: Bookmark https://security.microsoft.com. Pin it to your browser sidebar. From now on, this is your security home page. Wrapping up the series That closes Microsoft Defender Demystified. If you’ve followed along from Part 1, you should now be able to:
Name and distinguish every branch of the Microsoft Defender family Explain what each of the four Microsoft Defender XDR workloads does Describe how Microsoft Defender for Cloud differs from Microsoft Defender XDR, and when each applies Make a defensible licensing recommendation across small business, mid-market, and enterprise scenarios Open the Microsoft Defender portal and find any feature in under thirty seconds That’s enough foundation to take meaningful action in your own tenant. The next step is depth.
Where to go from here 🔗 Continue with the Microsoft Secure Score deep-dive series. You now know that Microsoft Secure Score lives inside Exposure management in the Defender portal. How We Built a Gold-Winning GRC Programme on Microsoft Secure Score turns that single feature into the engine of an award-winning ISO 27001 and NIS2 compliance programme, the same blueprint that won Gold at the Cyber Security Awards 2026.

Welcome to Part 4, the last one. Part 1 covered architecture, Part 2 covered discovery, Part 3 covered prioritization. We’ve identified the right vulnerabilities to fix. Now we get to Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management remediation, and equally important we wire MDVM into the rest of the security stack so the data doesn’t just live in one portal.
This is also where the Secure Score as Cyber GRC thread comes back in. If you’ve been following that series, the loop closes here.
The Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Remediation Workflow In MDVM, every Security Recommendation has a Request remediation button. This is the bread and butter, and it’s how most of the day-to-day work happens.
When you click Request remediation, you fill out a short form: which devices are in scope, what kind of action (update, configuration change, attention required), priority, due date, and notes. Submit, and a remediation ticket is created and tracked in MDVM itself.
Where it goes from there depends on your integrations.
With Intune integration enabled, and you should have this enabled, the ticket can flow into Intune as a remediation task. For supported software updates, Intune can apply the fix automatically using update rings, app deployments, or configuration profiles, and report back to MDVM when complete. The portal shows progress device-by-device. This is the “one-click remediation” you’ll see in Microsoft marketing, and it’s not entirely marketing, for in-scope scenarios, it works.
Without Intune integration, or for things Intune can’t fix, the ticket lives in MDVM as a tracking record. The remediating team reads it, fixes the issue out-of-band, and marks complete. MDVM still verifies the fix on its own schedule by re-evaluating the device.
The workflow that matters more than the technology: every remediation has an owner, a due date, and a verification step. That’s not a Microsoft thing, that’s a vulnerability management thing. MDVM gives you the surface; the discipline is yours.
ServiceNow integration For organizations running ServiceNow as the system of record for IT operations, MDVM integrates via Microsoft Graph. The pattern: a remediation request in MDVM creates a corresponding incident or change request in ServiceNow, owned by the right assignment group, tracked through your existing ITIL processes.
Setup is non-trivial, it involves a Graph application registration, ServiceNow’s MID Server, and field mappings, but the value is high for organizations that already live in ServiceNow. Auditors love seeing the same vulnerability reflected in both systems with consistent IDs.
If you’re not on ServiceNow but you’re on a different ITSM, the Graph API path (more on that below) lets you build a similar bridge with reasonable effort.
Exception management Sometimes you can’t fix the thing. The vendor hasn’t released a patch. The fix breaks a critical application. The device is going out of service in 60 days. Whatever the reason, MDVM supports exceptions: a documented decision to accept the risk, with an expiration date.
Two flavors:
Global exceptions: organization-wide exclusion of a recommendation. Per-device-group exceptions: scoped to a specific population. Two non-negotiables when you use exceptions.
Set an expiration date. “Permanent exception” is wrong every single time. The world changes, patches ship, devices retire, threats evolve. An exception that doesn’t expire is a vulnerability hidden by a process choice.
Write a real justification. “Business reasons” is not a justification. “Patch breaks the SAP HANA integration; vendor case 12345 open; mitigation in place via firewall ACL X” is a justification. Future you will thank present you when the auditor asks.
Exception hygiene is one of the cleanest indicators I know of vulnerability management maturity. Mature programs have a small, curated list of exceptions with clear expirations. Immature programs have a sea of “approved” exceptions that nobody has reviewed in two years.
Block Vulnerable Applications (Add-on) This one is underrated. With the Vulnerability Management Add-on, you can block a vulnerable application from running across your fleet, as a temporary mitigation while you work the patch. The block is enforced by Defender for Endpoint’s attack surface reduction layer.
When to use it:
A zero-day in a non-essential app, where you’d rather suspend usage than risk exposure for the days it takes to patch. A specific vulnerable version of an otherwise-essential app, when you can block just that version while users on newer versions continue working. An end-of-support app you’re trying to phase out, block it on devices where the migration is supposed to be done, see who screams, you’ve found your stragglers. Use carefully. Blocking an app users actually need will generate tickets fast. But for the right scenario, it’s the difference between exposed and not.
Security Baselines (Add-on) Now we’re at one of the most strategically important Add-on capabilities. Security Baselines Assessment evaluates every managed device against an established hardening baseline and tells you, control-by-control, where it conforms and where it doesn’t.
Out of the box, MDVM ships profiles for:
CIS Benchmarks for Windows, including Server and Workstation profiles at multiple levels. STIG profiles for Windows. And increasingly Linux and macOS coverage as Microsoft expands. You can also build custom profiles by selecting individual controls and adapting them to your environment. The classic case: you start from CIS Level 1, exclude the controls that don’t fit your business, and end up with a “Company X CIS-Adapted” baseline you can audit against repeatedly.
For the GRC readers: this is one of the cleanest controls-to-evidence pipelines Microsoft offers. You can point an ISO 27001 or NIS2 auditor at the Security Baselines dashboard and demonstrate, control-by-control, the state of your fleet. With timestamps. With device-level drill-down. Try doing that in a spreadsheet.
The maturity arc most organizations follow:
Pick a Microsoft-published profile (CIS Level 1 is a good start). Run it. Realize compliance is at 38%. Don’t panic. Triage the gaps. Some are real, some are spurious, some need exception decisions. Build a 90-day plan to drive compliance up. Track weekly. After a quarter, build your custom profile based on lessons learned. Advanced Hunting, KQL across MDVM data Defender XDR’s Advanced Hunting lets you query MDVM data with KQL (Kusto Query Language). The relevant tables are:
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory — every software product/version on every device DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities — every CVE found on every device DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilitiesKB — knowledge base of CVEs (severity, CVSS, threat insights) DeviceTvmSecureConfigurationAssessment — every configuration check on every device DeviceTvmSecureConfigurationAssessmentKB — knowledge base of configuration checks DeviceTvmInfoGathering and DeviceTvmInfoGatheringKB — additional context A few queries I keep on hand.
Find devices with active exploit + critical CVE:
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | join kind=inner DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilitiesKB on CveId | where VulnerabilitySeverityLevel == "Critical" | where IsExploitAvailable == true | summarize DeviceCount = dcount(DeviceId) by CveId, VulnerabilityDescription | order by DeviceCount desc Find devices missing a specific CVE patch:
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId == "CVE-2025-XXXXX" | project DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion Configuration drift over time:
DeviceTvmSecureConfigurationAssessment | where ConfigurationId == "scid-2010" // example: BitLocker | where IsCompliant == false | summarize NonCompliantDevices = dcount(DeviceId) by bin(Timestamp, 1d) | render timechart These tables are also queryable from Microsoft Sentinel if you’ve enabled the Defender XDR connector, same data, same KQL, different portal.
Microsoft Graph Security API For programmatic access (custom dashboards, in-house tooling, automation) MDVM data is exposed through the Microsoft Graph Security API. The relevant endpoints cover security recommendations, vulnerabilities, secure configurations, and device-level data.
Common automation patterns:
Custom executive dashboards that pull MDVM data into Power BI or Grafana for an audience that doesn’t live in Defender XDR. CMDB sync, push asset criticality from your CMDB into MDVM device tagging. Ticket creation in non-ServiceNow ITSMs. Compliance reporting that combines MDVM data with other GRC sources. If you have Power BI, Microsoft also publishes template apps for vulnerability management reporting, which give you a starting dashboard you can customize. Faster than building from scratch.
Sentinel pipeline integration For SOCs running Microsoft Sentinel, MDVM data flows in via the Defender XDR connector. Once connected, the same DeviceTvm* tables are available in your Sentinel workspace, joinable with your other ingested logs.
The high-value pattern: enrich your incidents with vulnerability context. A Sentinel alert fires on a device. Your detection rule joins to DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities to ask, “what unpatched CVEs does this device have right now?” The analyst opens the incident with that context already attached. Triage time drops, decision quality goes up.
This is the kind of integration that doesn’t show up in the marketing slide, it’s plumbing, but it’s where day-to-day SOC value compounds.
Closing the GRC loop, MDVM and Microsoft Secure Score For those of you reading the Secure Score as Cyber GRC series, this is the convergence point.
Microsoft Secure Score (the tenant-wide one, in security.microsoft.com) is a posture score across the whole Microsoft 365 environment, Identity, Devices, Apps, Data. Each “Improvement Action” in Secure Score is worth points; implementing it raises your score; auditors and boards are increasingly asking about it.
A meaningful chunk of Secure Score Improvement Actions in the Devices category are sourced from MDVM. Examples:
“Update operating system to latest version”, driven by MDVM software inventory and CVE assessment. “Enable Network Protection in block mode”, a configuration assessment surfaced through MDVM. “Set BitLocker drive encryption”, a configuration baseline check. “Block executable content from email client and webmail”, an ASR rule, evaluated by MDVM configuration assessment. So the data flow is: MDVM detects → Secure Score scores → improvement action lights up → you remediate (often via Intune, often triggered from MDVM) → MDVM verifies → Secure Score updates.
If you’ve been wondering how to operationalize Secure Score, this is the answer. Secure Score is the executive view; MDVM is the operational engine. The same actions that move Secure Score also reduce Exposure Score. The same evidence that satisfies an internal stakeholder satisfies an external auditor.
This is the loop that takes Microsoft Secure Score from “a number on a slide” to “a defensible measurement of cyber posture, backed by device-level evidence, traceable to specific GRC controls.” That’s the GRC instrument framing the other series builds out in detail.
A Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management Maturity Model Where do you go from here? A rough four-stage model I use with clients:
Stage 1 — Visibility. MDE deployed, MDVM lit up, inventory accurate, Exposure Score being watched. Most organizations stall here for too long.
Stage 2 — Triage. Threat Insights and Breach Insights filters in active use. Tuesday-morning routine in place. Asset value tags applied to high-value devices. Remediation requests flowing into Intune for in-scope cases.
Stage 3 — Baselines. Add-on enabled. Security Baselines profile selected (CIS or STIG). Compliance trending up over quarters. Exception register clean and reviewed.
Stage 4 — Integration. MDVM data flowing into Sentinel and/or Power BI. Custom KQL hunts running. Secure Score actively managed as a board-level metric. Auditor evidence packs generated from MDVM dashboards.
There’s no shortcut. Stage 1 takes a quarter, Stage 2 takes another, Stage 3 takes longer, Stage 4 is where you live for years. The reward is that the 4-hour problem stops being a slogan in a LinkedIn post and starts being a measured, controlled operational reality.
Wrapping the series We started this series with one number: 4 hours. The window between disclosure and exploitation, in 2024, on average. The window that’s projected to get smaller every year.
MDVM doesn’t make that window go away. Nothing will. What MDVM does is collapse your side of the window, the time between “a vulnerability appears in your environment” and “the right person knows, with the context to act.”
For a small team without a dedicated vulnerability manager, that collapse is the difference between getting hit and not. For a large team with mature processes, it’s the difference between burning out chasing CVSS 9.8s and actually making your environment harder.
Either way, the engine is in your tenant already, mostly licensed, mostly under-used. Go use it.
If you found this series useful, the natural next read is Secure Score as Cyber GRC, where MDVM data feeds the GRC instrument story. Or jump into Defender Demystified for the wider Defender for Endpoint context.
Thanks for reading. Questions, corrections, and “hey you got this wrong” notes, always welcome. The fastest way to reach me is LinkedIn.
— Dimosthenis
